title: Holding the door — and staying to hold it
description: Holding a door takes three seconds and costs nothing, yet people remember it all day. The small courtesy works because of what it quietly says: I saw you, and you matter enough to wait for.

body.heading: The three-second courtesy
paragraphs: A held door helps in obvious ways — arms full of shopping, a pushchair, a walking stick — but its real payload is acknowledgement. Being noticed by a stranger, and treated as worth a pause, reliably lifts people's mood far beyond the size of the act.
The full version includes staying to hold it: stepping with the door rather than letting it swing from a stretched arm, and meeting the person's eye as they pass.

body.heading: Courtesies that chain
paragraphs: Small kindnesses are contagious in a practical sense: people who have just been helped are more likely to help the next person they meet. One held door can echo down a corridor of strangers all morning.
None of this needs a programme or a budget. It needs only the habit of looking up — at doors, lifts and crossings — for the person coming behind you.

takeaway: Holding a door, and staying to hold it, is a three-second act of acknowledgement that people remember — and pass on.
